To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the contribution of seed vectors (birds and mice) to the fitness of wild rose (Rosa canina L.) is largely independent of the dispersal-related traits of the plants and their avian seed dispersers and is determined by the relative importance of reproductive depression caused by ungulate browsing and by mice seed predation.

the contribution of avian seed-disper- sers to the fitness of a wild rose species in the field is not related to their dispersal-related plant trait values, but is instead the result of complex interactions between the plant, the seed dispersers and other biotic and abiotic factors.

the fitness consequences of seed dispersal are ultimately determined by factors not directly linked to the interaction between the plant and its seed-dispersal vectors, and that the contribution of seed dispersal to plant fitness may be either positive, neutral, or negative depending on whether or not reproductive depression by browsing ungulates is compensated by seed predation by birds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the ecological and evolutionary consequences of seed dispersal in a wild plant species.
the combined effects of seed predators and browsers on the seed-dispersal system of a plant species.
the factors affecting the fitness of Rosa plants in the wild and the contribution of their avian seed vectors to this fitness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the contribution of seed vectors (birds and mice) to the fitness of R. canina plants is neutral or slightly positive, depending on the relative contribution of ungulates, and the relative importance of reproductive depression (pre-disperser) and seed predation (post-disperser).
, in the case of Rosa, birds are not good dispersers.
the average contribution of avian dispersers to the fitness of their host plant is neutral or slightly positive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the average contribution of birds to Rosa fitness is neutral, whereas that of hawthorns is positive.

, in spite of the high level of specialization of birds as seed-dispersers of haws and the high level of coevolution between the two groups, the ultimate fitness of the plant depends on a number of factors that are not directly related to the interaction between the two groups.
the contribution of seed vectors is largely neutral for Rosa, but it is strongly negative in the absence of ungulate and mouse control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to understand the evolution of plant traits, we need to consider the effects of other organisms on plants and the effects of plants on other organisms.

the contribution of seed vectors (birds) to the fitness of a plant species may be either positive or negative and may even be neutral, depending on the relative contribution of the reproductive depression by ungulates and mice.
seed dispersal is an ecological process with important implications for plant fitness and population dynamics, which should be studied in a broader ecological context.
